item.title: AI contract management: What CIOs should look for
item.description:
Imagine a salesperson getting ready for a customer renewal meeting. They need to find the original contract and review its terms. But the information is buried in CRM records and attachments, forcing them to search through multiple documents.

Now imagine they could simply type in their question and get the contract details in seconds. Contracts contain valuable business information, including pricing, payment terms, and past negotiations. AI for contract management helps teams find and use that information — and connects it to the work that follows, from reviewing terms to getting approvals and preparing for renewals.

Foundry’s 2026 State of the CIO research reports that 79% of CIOs are working more closely with business leaders on AI applications. Contracting is a practical place to put that collaboration to work: sales, legal, procurement, and HR all depend on contracts to move business forward.

Docusign is using AI-powered contract management across its own business through its Docusign Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM), its AI contracting platform. The goal is to connect contract information with everyday workflows while keeping people involved in decisions that require judgment.

“AI contract management helps our teams turn what’s inside contracts into action,” said Shanthi Iyer, CIO of Docusign. “Using our own IAM platform, we’re automating routine workflows so people can focus their expertise where it matters most — and stay in control of the decisions. That means less friction for our teams and a better experience for our customers.”

How does AI contract management work?

AI contract management combines AI capabilities — such as analyzing contract language and extracting important information — with workflows that help teams create, review, approve, sign, and manage contracts. For example, AI can help flag language that differs from company standards or find a renewal deadline, while connected workflows route the contract or task to the right person.

Docusign delivers these capabilities through IAM. For organizations with complex contracting needs, the platform includes advanced Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM) capabilities. Iris, Docusign’s AI engine built specifically for contracts, powers AI-assisted review, an AI assistant, and agents that help teams understand contracts and move work forward. IAM also helps organizations analyze past contracts to prepare for renewals and negotiate better terms.

By making contract data accessible within business systems, IAM helps employees find information and complete tasks faster. A 2026 study by Deloitte and Docusign found that organizations using AI and automated contract workflows saw average efficiency gains of 36%.

Deploying AI and contract automation across the enterprise

Docusign uses its AI and contract automation to help employees find contract information and act on it. Here’s how different areas of the business benefit:

  • Sales: The sales team uses natural-language queries to find contract terms and deal history, reporting approximately 50% productivity gains and reclaiming 42,000 hours annually.
  • Procurement: Finding supplier contracts now takes under one minute, compared with over eight minutes previously.
  • Legal: The legal team uses AI-assisted review and playbooks to flag nonstandard terms, allowing attorneys to spend more time on negotiations.
  • HR: Integrating IAM with Workday connects contractor statements of work to onboarding, helping HR get new contractors started with less manual work.
  • Customer experience and partner operations: The customer marketing team collects speaker releases and consent forms through IAM, saving roughly 200 hours annually. Partner operations use IAM with Salesforce to initiate due diligence checks, saving 10–15 minutes per review.

What CIOs should look for in an AI contracting platform

Here are some questions to ask when evaluating an AI contracting solution:

  • Can it support everyday workflows? Ask for a demonstration of a familiar task, such as reviewing an NDA, routing a sales contract for approval, or preparing for a supplier renewal. Examine how information moves from one step to the next.
  • Does it integrate with existing systems? Check how contract data and tasks move between tools such as CRM, procurement, and HR systems — and whether employees can access them where they already work.
  • Can it provide appropriate controls and visibility? Examine access permissions and review processes.
  • Can you measure its impact? Track process completion times before and after implementation.

Turning contract intelligence into business advantage

CIOs should consider how AI contract management can help their organizations get more value from contracts long after they’re signed. Docusign’s experience demonstrates that contracts can become a valuable source of information for future business decisions.

Discover how Docusign’s AI contracting platform helps teams create, review, sign, and manage contracts—and put contract information to work across the enterprise.

item.title: HP’s next CEO loves confrontation
item.description:
The new year will see a new CEO for HP, which after a nine-month search has named Emma Walmsley to lead the company from January 4, 2027.

Walmsley was previously CEO of drug company GSK, where she turned around its finances and spun off its consumer healthcare business into a new company, Haleon. She has a reputation for courting confrontation rather than yes-men in the boardroom. HP needs a shake-up as revenue from printing declines and AI-driven demand for components is forcing up PC prices.

She will take over from HP’s interim CEO Bruce Broussard, who stepped in in February when former CEO Enrique Lores left the company after more than 25 years to become president and CEO at PayPal. There’s a consolation prize for Broussard, who will become chair of HP’s board, succeeding Chip Bergh who remains a board member.

Although Walmsley has been on Microsoft’s board for seven years (she is stepping down in December), this is her first foray into leading a tech company. Her almost 16-year tenure at GSK included more than eight years as CEO, and earlier in her career, she spent 17 years at L’Oréal.

Bergh said that during the executive search, she stood out “for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth.” He particularly cited her people-first leadership approach.

Walmsley reiterated her commitment to the philosophy in a post on LinkedIn. “HP has an extraordinary innovation heritage, an inspiring purpose and an incredible opportunity ahead as AI reshapes technology and what customers need from it. I’m excited to build on those strengths and help translate innovation into impact,” she wrote. “Behind every innovation are the people who work to make someone’s day a little easier, their work more productive, their ideas possible. In an age of AI, I believe human leadership has never mattered more. It’s a privilege to be joining this team.”

Announcing Walmsley’s appointment Broussard said, “We need a leader who can build on our innovation heritage and strengths to boldly shape the company’s future. Emma is a proven CEO with a track record of leading organizations at scale and guiding them through significant change. She has the experience and skills to bring HP’s businesses, capabilities, and people together to capture the opportunities ahead as AI moves to the edge, transforming how we work and live in a more connected world.”

This article first appeared on Computerworld.

item.title: How to balance governance and innovation in the agentic AI era
item.description:
The conversation about agentic AI is shifting: Rather than focusing solely on what the technology can produce, IT leaders are now considering what they are prepared to let it do. 

Unlike traditional AI assistants that primarily respond to user prompts, agentic AI systems can make decisions and execute actions autonomously across business processes. This creates opportunities to accelerate workflows and improve productivity but also introduces new challenges involving risk and organizational readiness.

The shift is already well under way. In a recent HCLTech survey, 87% of the participating enterprises reported using generative or agentic AI in IT operations, underscoring the growing importance of effective governance. These challenges were central to a recent HCLTech and Google Cloud roundtable on the business impact of agentic AI in which the participants explored what it takes to move from experimentation toward enterprise-wide adoption.

Agentic AI is showing promise across a wide range of business functions, including IT operations, software engineering, customer experience, HR, marketing, finance, and sustainability. Across these areas, intelligent agents can streamline complex workflows; automate routine tasks; and support faster, more informed decision-making.

Realizing potential

But realizing that potential requires more than deploying new technology. Successful implementations begin with identifying high-value use cases, establishing measurable key performance indicators (KPIs), and connecting AI initiatives to specific business outcomes.

Roundtable participants highlighted concerns about cost, ROI, and insufficient testing, reinforcing the importance of a measured approach to adoption. To manage these risks, organizations are typically starting with lower-risk business processes, demonstrating tangible value before expanding their use of autonomous agents as confidence and capabilities mature. Those concerns are reflected in HCLTech’s AI Impact Imperatives 2026 research, conducted by Omdia, which found that respondents expect approximately 43% of their major AI initiatives to fail.

Rethinking governance for autonomous systems

As AI moves from assisting employees to acting on their behalf, traditional approaches to governance and compliance may prove inadequate. Autonomous agents introduce operational and reputational risks that require organizations to reconsider how decisions are monitored, audited, and controlled.

Governance must be built into agentic AI initiatives from the outset rather than added after deployment. That includes establishing clear boundaries for autonomous agents and determining where human intervention remains necessary. Human oversight is particularly important in high-stakes areas such as financial transactions, regulatory compliance, cybersecurity, and decisions affecting customers or employees. The appropriate level of oversight should reflect the potential business impact and risk associated with an agent’s actions.

Clear accountability, transparent decision-making, and escalation mechanisms can help organizations balance greater autonomy with continued human control over critical decisions.

Preparing for new ways of working

Technology alone won’t determine whether agentic AI succeeds at enterprise scale. Organizational readiness is another major hurdle, requiring businesses to align data, governance, people, and processes around common objectives. Change management and AI literacy are particularly important. Employees across technical and nontechnical roles will need new skills to supervise agents, evaluate their decisions, and collaborate effectively with autonomous systems.

As agents become increasingly integrated into business operations, organizations will also need to reconsider how their performance is managed and measured. Over the next several years, enterprises may see the emergence of hybrid teams in which employees focus more heavily on strategic decisions and oversight while AI agents take on more operational responsibilities.

Achieving this vision will require organizations to rethink operating models and invest in workforce readiness alongside technology. Ultimately, the autonomous enterprise will be defined by how effectively AI agents are integrated into business operations and deliver measurable results, rather than simply by how many agents an organization deploys.

Learn more about how HCLTech and Google Cloud are helping enterprises navigate the transition to agentic AI.

item.title: AI agent autonomy remains an elusive work in progress
item.description:
The true promise of agentic AI lies in agents maneuvering, making decisions, and taking actions autonomously throughout the enterprise, but few IT leaders appear ready to give bots widespread control.

According to a KPMG survey from July and August, 62% of IT leaders reported they were building, deploying, or developing AI agents, up from 53% in the previous quarter. But many IT leaders still say they are uncomfortable with the prospect of turning over internal processes to agents, with some exceptions for basic, low-risk functions like tier 1 IT support.

Jim Olsen, CTO of AI lifecycle management and governance vendor ModelOp, sees agent autonomy making inroads in limited circumstances — for example, to process customer refunds or credits without human intervention. But early lessons in the risks of full autonomy remain top of mind for IT leaders.

“We saw the large adoption of Clawdbot and OpenClaw by individuals where they would allow it full access to their email and gave it full autonomy,” he says. “For some people that worked out well, but it was a large risk exposure.”

For IT leaders deploying autonomous bots, Olsen recommends confining them to a strict sandbox with well-defined policies to limit their autonomy.

“I do not see allowing agents full and complete autonomy to do whatever they want being used in an enterprise in the near future,” he says. “But restricted autonomy is, in fact, already in use today.”

Activities that aren’t mission critical and don’t have access to sensitive information will be where IT leaders first grant agents full autonomy, Olsen predicts. “As trust improves, so will the breadth of use cases,” he adds.

Some IT leaders are concerned about “autonomy creep,” when agents quietly take more authority than they are given. And many AI and security experts warn that human-in-the-loop guardrails don’t always give employees the authority or time needed to fix agent errors.

Still, IT leaders have several methods for enforcing runtime policies and keeping agent behavior within acceptable goals, including API gateways, OS-level enforcement, and credential management, Olsen says.

“This means having clear policies in place and being able to tie them to the specific agent and use case,” he adds. “Some of these solutions are available now, but a more overall cohesive strategy is needed to bring about this minimal level of trust.”

Defining the sweet spot for autonomy

With about 2,000 agents deployed within her enterprise, Siroui Mushegian, CIO of cybersecurity vendor Barracuda Networks, still has human employees checking bot actions.

“We have many agents that are very close [to autonomous] — many of our ticketing automations are in the ‘trust-but-verify’ category with the agents that oversee them,” she says. “The more we see success, the greater comfort we have, but I am still not 100% certain I want to allow zero human accountability, especially when it comes to auditable processes.”

Mushegian expects autonomy to expand as agents demonstrate they can handle specific tasks reliably. “The consequences of a mistake should determine how much evidence you need before giving an agent more authority,” she says.

Autonomy will likely come to agents executing specific tasks within a function, she adds. Routine internal support requests are a reasonable candidate for autonomy when the answer is well documented, the action is limited, and a mistake is straightforward to correct, she suggests.

Less likely candidates for autonomy are agents that can change access permissions or make changes to a production system, Mushegian adds.

“Even within one workflow, an agent might complete some steps on its own and need approval for others,” she says. “I’d give it only the authority it needs for the task, with human approval for decisions where a mistake could have serious consequences.”

It’s about the action, not the agent

Joshua Rowe, co-founder and CTO of household bills app provider Taupia, agrees that IT leaders shouldn’t give agents complete freedom in every circumstance.

“I’d draw the line at the action rather than the agent,” he says. “The same agent can act alone on one step and need sign-off on the next.”

However, Rowe sees a lot of areas where agents can run near-autonomously right now, including read-heavy work such as gathering data, triage, drafting, and comparing options.

Taupia is testing agent functionality that compares energy deals and takes steps to allow customers to switch providers without its employees approving each step. However, the customer still would have to review the change and confirm it before it goes into effect.

For agents to get autonomous authority for irreversible actions, the timeframe doesn’t depend on AI models getting smarter, Rowe says.

“It depends on how quickly an organization can make each action reversible or bounded, with spending limits, cooling-off periods, rollback, and an audit trail good enough to undo a mistake,” he says. “Once an action has those, it can go autonomous. Where it can’t be undone, like signing a contract or moving money out of an account, I’d keep a person approving it for the foreseeable future.”

A question of deliberate design

Maciej Walaszczyk, CTO at AI customer service platform provider Text, points to customer service as an area where IT leaders have begun to cede control to agents.

“In customer service, which is my field of expertise, agents can indeed answer customer inquiries without the need for constant supervision, as they learn from knowledge provided by humans,” he says. “The scope of autonomy depends on permissions and the consequences of an action. Furthermore, the scope of these responses can be tailored to specific needs.”

But Walaszczyk says he would not hand entire departments over to agents. Instead, IT leaders should delegate specific processes where they can define the goal, set boundaries, and verify the outcomes, he recommends.

“An agent acting on my behalf cannot have more authority than I do,” he adds. “I don’t think it’s a question of being comfortable or even courageous, but of deliberately designing the environment, permissions, instructions, and oversight.”

Trust will come from real work and verified results, and humans must remain in the loop to check agent outcomes in many cases, Walaszczyk adds.

“Oversight must be real,” he says. “It takes time and attention, and it means much more than clicking approve. Saying ‘AI did it’ does not remove their responsibility. Irreversible actions or those with major consequences require human review.”

item.title: Lessons learned: Common engineering pitfalls to avoid in the age of AI
item.description:
A LinkedIn post about my old company, insightsoftware, popped up the other day. It was lamenting the challenge of turning 29 acquisitions and close to 80 products into one comprehensive platform. I spent years in the middle of that work, and what I know now is how much harder that consolidation is than you might think, and how much of it you only learn by getting it wrong first. 

So, when I arrived at Veson in November and found a similar landscape, I felt a bit of déjà vu. A bit of “I’ve done this before, so I know what I’m doing” and a bit of “I’ve done this before and I know it’s no cakewalk.” Veson had spent the past several years acquiring a range of products like Shipfix and VesselsValue and now needed to consolidate them onto a platform alongside its flagship IMOS solution. A new variable is also now at play that changes the whole equation: the advancement of AI.

While AI may sound like a cheat code for this work, it’s very much a double-edged sword… with a grenade taped to it. 

Yes, we can do some things faster and differently than we ever could a few years ago. But we’re also learning as we go and upskilling our team as we go, on a technology that’s changing under our feet.

The newness of these tools multiplies the complexity in a way I didn’t fully appreciate at insightsoftware. Back then, the tools simply didn’t exist or were just emerging. Now your platform must transform so that it thrives in the age of AI. It has to be built in the age of AI, which — depending on whose study you believe — means anywhere from 2X to 10X faster.

And then your team needs to adapt to the age of AI, which again means faster, at higher quality and producing more output. That’s a lot of spinning plates, on top of each other, none of which you’re allowed to drop. 

Oh, and one other plate: this is a centuries-old industry that moves billions of dollars in freight a year and does not stop for anyone. You don’t get to tie the ship up at the dock while you rebuild the engine. Business continuity, zero migration, no breaking the thing people are already running their business on. And do it as fast as you possibly can. 

Building a connected, modern platform

At Veson we had a fleet, not a unified experience. A set of strong, separate hulls, each with its own data, its own experience, its own idea of the world. A collection of great products is not the same as a cohesive foundation, and pretending otherwise is a mistake. I’ve been guilty of this myself: combining products superficially, so they sit side by side under one roof but still behave as separate entities, rather than as one integrated experience.

In fairness to my past self, before AI even that superficial stitching was slow, labor-intensive and risky, and it often used up the time and budget we’d meant for real integration. AI has worn much of that cost away. The plumbing that used to take months now takes weeks, which frees us to focus on what customers value most: products that work as one.

A platform, in 2026, is three things stacked in order. A singular data layer underneath. One experience on top. And then AI that can reason across all of it. You cannot bolt credible AI onto a flotilla; it has nothing coherent to reason over. The unglamorous work of unifying data is what makes the glamorous AI work possible. 

The part I’m most wary of talking about — because I would rather not tempt fate — is doing all of this safely. Moving fast on all fronts at once is a lovely thing to say in a strategy meeting and a dangerous thing to do in production. The mistake I’ve watched happen (and, if I’m honest, helped cause) is measuring efficacy too narrowly.

If you pick only a few metrics (that you know you can nail) and tell people that’s how they’ll be judged, teams will act accordingly. The side effects get ignored or missed until it’s too late. Often that side effect is quality, discovered downstream when it’s far costlier to fix, or market fit, because value was quietly descoped to hit a date. With AI coding agents accelerating everything, I wasn’t willing to repeat that. We needed 360-degree checks and balances.

The one thing I insisted on and set up from the first week with Veson was working with the engineering intelligence platform Plandek. We measure speed, quality, predictability and focus in real time, so we can see the progress we’re making and spot the side effects before they compound.

AI let us pick up the pace; comprehensive measurement is what lets us keep it without losing sight of the risk. As a result, we get to have our cake and eat it, we upskill the team while the ship is sailing.

Ten months in, here’s what we’ve learned so far.

Product lessons we’ve learned

  • Don’t rebuild what already works. “Modernizing” something people rely on is the fastest way to destroy the value you paid for. 
  • AI only counts when it functions inside a workflow people already trust. An assistant in a corner nobody visits is a demo, not a product. 
  • Aim for a minimum lovable product, not a minimum viable one.
  • Continuity is a feature. The moment a customer must “migrate” to your platform, you’ve lost them. 
  • One source of truth beats five clever ones. Data you unify late is a tax you pay forever. 

Experiences from our engineering teams 

  • Adoption will be uneven. Don’t force the sceptics; convert them with proof. 
  • The job itself is changing from writing code to directing it — reviewing, steering and trusting AI as it writes, then verifying. 
  • Spread what works peer to peer. A network of AI champions beats a mandate from someone who clearly hasn’t done the work. 
  • Measure everything. 
  • The fastest teams are the ones who trust the platform beneath them. 
  • Faster is only a win if quality holds — protect the gates hardest exactly when the pressure to cut them is highest. 

I don’t think we’ve cracked the code on this. We’re in the middle of it, plates still spinning. But this time I’m making new mistakes rather than old ones, and I’m more convinced than ever that we’re doing this the right way.

item.title: Building the IT organization that anticipates what’s next
item.description:
For decades, CIOs have been challenging their organizations to shed one of the most persistent labels in our profession: order taker. Instead of waiting for the business to tell them what they want, technology leaders need to understand what the business is trying to accomplish, get invited into the first meeting, and earn the right to become a strategic partner. But in a fast-moving environment, is being a trusted advisor enough?

To reach the next level, top CIOs are increasingly transforming their IT organizations into what I call “innovative anticipators”: These IT orgs understand the business, customer, and possibilities so deeply that they can see around corners, anticipate what’s needed next, and create value before someone asks for it.

Janet Robertson, global CIO of RS Group, believes building that anticipation muscle isn’t simply about moving the IT organization to a higher level of maturity. Increasingly, it’s a business imperative.

For a recent episode of the Tech Whisperers podcast, Robertson and I explored the deeply human side of leadership: how trust goes both ways, how great leaders serve as a lighthouse when others are navigating through the fog, and how we prepare the next generation to lead in a world none of us has led in before. But hiding inside that conversation was another fascinating story to unpack.

RS Group is a global product and service solutions provider for industrial customers operating in 33 markets. Its journey has been remarkably similar to the one our IT profession has been making — from taking orders, to advising customers, to anticipating what they might need next. As Robertson evolves IT at RS into an innovative anticipator, the company as a whole is doing the same.

Two journeys, similar challenges. And as Robertson explains in the following conversation, strategic partnership may no longer be the destination for today’s CIO. It may be the starting point for what comes next.

Dan Roberts: You’ve said something that sounds simple but has enormous implications: There isn’t a technology strategy and a business strategy. There’s one business strategy. What changes in the way a technology organization operates when people genuinely believe that?

Janet Robertson: When the technology group is focused on an outcome, they’re looking at solving a business problem more than implementing a technical solution. That’s a nuance, but it’s really the most direct route to a solution, because they’re trying to solve a business problem and get a business outcome more than implementing a technology solution or a technology transformation. It’s a different mindset.

In practical terms, you end up with increased adoption because you’ve got buy-in from the business on the direct answer to the problem. You also end up with fewer bells and whistles — a solution that’s not gold-plated and that doesn’t have things you won’t need, which is more efficient, considering how fast things are moving today. Everything could be different.

In fact, we’re doing product development now as more of a continuous evolution using new, innovative tools that are available to us at each space. The days of planning a three- or four-year program are over. By the time you’re going live, the technology’s out of date, or the processes have changed, or the world’s changed around it. You’ve got to create solutions fast with the most direct available technology to support the business outcomes.

You can’t anticipate a business you only understand through dashboards. How do you get your technology leaders close enough to the work, the customers, and the people to see what they otherwise might miss?

I encourage my leaders to spend time in the everyday working life of the recipients of our solutions. Sit with some of our biggest customers and watch them place an order through our website. Sit with our middle- and back-office team and watch their process of paying an invoice, receiving an order, entering an order, processing an order. Go to the distribution center. Spend time with the people who are using your solution.

Our customer experience officer has been riding around with salespeople, experiencing what they are going through in a day-to-day environment. I’m going out to Milan, Italy, next week to open our new our automated warehouse there. I’m almost more excited about launching it and seeing what we’ve implemented in use than I was planning the program. I want to see the ship sail in clear waters.

When technology leaders spend the time doing this, they start to see the connection directly between what they’re putting out there and what actually has to take place. You get very different perspectives from different sides of the fence when you get hands-on. It’s less about KPIs and dashboards and the results out of the other end of it. It’s more about understanding who’s consuming what you’re producing and how you’re providing value to them. Because sometimes, their biggest pain point is something you put down as a priority 5, and it’s in the lowest level of the backlog, but would completely change their perspective, improve their experience, and drive value.

What have the best consumer experiences taught you about orchestrating a B2B customer experience that will continue to differentiate RS Group?

Our catalog is massive, and we’ve got so much to navigate. As a consumer, with the new developments you can go on to an Amazon experience and find anything you want using even cryptic keywords. Or you can go on to Google and find 20 different buying options. That is absolutely transformative for us, because a lot of our customers buy that way. They’re searching for something that’s maybe very specialized, so they expect the same kind of Amazon-type experience when they’re looking for a specialized manufacturing-line repair part.

For us in the technology space, it means we’ve got to make sure that our data and our foundations are prepared to enable those large language models for the AI and generative search for agentic purchasing. What’s a little bit different from the B2C space is that many of our customers are starting to implement agents to do a lot of their procurement. So we’ve got to be prepared on the receiving end of those agents to be able to place those digital orders. It’s not really an e-commerce, add-to-cart channel anymore. Now it’s a direct agentic experience in purchasing for our bigger customers that use agentic purchasing.

To lead the way on that is a huge differentiator, and we are aware of it, and we’re keeping an eye on it. We have to be able to move fast and pivot quickly. Who would have thought two years ago that we were going to be talking to agentic procurement?

For years, we’ve challenged IT organizations to do a better job demonstrating their value to the business and to become trusted advisors. How has your organization made that pivot, and what does the next evolution of that journey look like?

When I first joined RS, my department was seen as less of a technical advisor or an expert in new technologies and new ways of getting things done. We were seen more as order takers and a cost center, basically a necessary evil. The pivot we’ve gone through has happened by listening and engaging with the business to understand and help them articulate what problems they’re truly trying to solve. I say, “Please tell me the what, and let me and my experts provide you the how.”

It’s taken some time, honestly. That evolution from an order taker to a trusted advisor is a journey, because you’ve got to prove that you know what you’re talking about, that you’re up on the latest technology, you understand the latest tools, and you are thinking outside of the box — truly providing the vision and the art of the possible to a problem they don’t know how to articulate. The biggest driver for me is connecting my leaders and my team to the business in general. They’re out looking for tools to solve those business problems.

Now we’re starting to partner with our business partners to show them the art of the possible with some of the new trends that are coming, like agentic procurement and large language model search. SEO is gone; now it’s GEO, generative engine optimization. So instead of “Tell me your business problem,” it’s moving to “Let me tell you how to solve a problem you might not know you have yet. This is a way to anticipate what is probably coming down the pipeline, and it’s going to be a problem soon.”

Because we’re leading the way in talking to our business about where the future’s going in technology and customer search and customer analytics and data science, we’re being brought in to discuss these developing trends.

That level of anticipation requires intelligence, or what you’ve described as “intelligent automation.” What’s involved in building that kind of anticipation engine?

Just like you can’t expect a 300-year-old house to be a smart house overnight, you can’t turn a 100-year-old business into an efficient, highly data-connected enterprise overnight. We know that we’ve got some legacy plumbing that we need to repair, and we are well into that journey now. We know that the data we have is incredibly valuable, but we need to understand how to use it, how to interrogate it, and how to get the right answers out of it. Without a structured format, and without all the speed and the pipes and efficient use, we can’t take advantage of that.

Bad data and a bad foundation only accentuate bad decision-making from the data. If you put a lot of intelligence over the top of an unstructured or bad format and foundation, you get really bad data to make decisions from, and it just makes it that much worse. So sometimes you have to build a little bit of a foundation before you’re able to just run with it.

For years, the goal for technology organizations was to become the trusted advisor who gets invited to the first meeting, not just be handed requirements after the important decisions have been made. Robertson’s experience suggests that today’s CIOs need to challenge their organizations to go further, from “Tell me what you’re trying to accomplish” to “Let me show you what’s coming.” That requires getting close enough to your business colleagues and customers to see what they may not see yet. It’s the difference between being invited to the first meeting and being the reason the meeting gets called.

For more from Janet Robertson’s leadership playbook, tune in to the Tech Whisperers.

See also:

  • IT reinvention requires mastering the art of translation
  • What separates true enterprise leaders from strong tech execs
  • The 7 new Cs of IT leadership for the AI era

item.title: Quantum without the hype: The CIO’s next architecture challenge
item.description:
The most expensive quantum mistake a CIO could make today may not be investing too early. It may be investing in the wrong capabilities, for the wrong reasons, without understanding the architectural and economic consequences.

Over decades of leading enterprise technology, architecture, modernization, and innovation in complex, highly regulated environments, I have seen a recurring pattern: technological enthusiasm advances faster than institutional readiness. Capital gets committed. Platforms become entrenched. Dependencies multiply. Business value remains difficult to demonstrate.

Quantum computing risks repeating that pattern, but with an important distinction: The cybersecurity consequences demand action today, while the timing and economics of broader commercial quantum advantage remain uncertain.

That is the strategic tension CIOs must resolve.

Quantum readiness and preparedness is not a race to acquire qubits. It is a discipline of protecting enterprise trust, preserving strategic options and directing scarce capital toward demonstrable value.

The fundamental question is no longer whether quantum computing deserves executive attention. It is whether CIOs and enterprises can distinguish what must be protected now, what deserves experimentation and what should remain an option rather than a financial commitment.

Two quantum clocks. One enterprise balance sheet

Quantum presents two fundamentally different timelines to a CIO.

The first is the security clock.

In August 2024, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published its first three finalized post-quantum cryptography standards, establishing practical mechanisms for protecting information against anticipated quantum-enabled threats.

This is critical because cryptography is not an isolated cybersecurity component. It underpins identities, financial transactions, digital signatures, software integrity, communications, connected infrastructure and trusted business relationships.

A sufficiently capable future quantum computer could compromise certain widely deployed public-key cryptographic methods.

The October 2026 U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, Quantum Computing: Federal Actions Needed to Prepare for Emerging Cyber Threat, reinforces the urgency. None of the 24 federal agencies examined had fully addressed all three assessed preparatory practices for migrating vulnerable cryptography.

The lesson extends beyond government: you cannot migrate cryptographic dependencies you have not discovered.

The second is the commercial advantage clock.

Quantum computing may eventually offer meaningful advantages in selected areas of chemistry, materials science, simulation and optimization. But promising research does not automatically translate into repeatable enterprise economics.

IBM’s published quantum technology roadmap targets a fault-tolerant quantum system in 2029. That is an important technological ambition, not a guaranteed date for widespread commercial advantage.

These two clocks should not share the same investment assumptions.

Security readiness is justified by exposure and risk tolerance. Commercial adoption must be justified by demonstrated advantage and economic returns.

Confusing the two creates either dangerous underinvestment or speculative overspending for the CIOs.

Architecture before acquisition

The enterprise architecture challenge is more consequential than the quantum procurement question.

For CIOs, post-quantum preparation begins with initial understanding of where vulnerable cryptography exists across their enterprise, how it supports critical business services and whether those dependencies can be changed without destabilizing operations.

For example, consider a globally distributed financial institution.

Cryptographic dependencies may span payment platforms, customer identities, authentication services, certificates, mainframes, cloud environments, third-party APIs and decades of retained information.

Replacing an algorithm is not necessarily equivalent to replacing a library.

Some changes affect protocols, hardware security modules, certificate lifecycles, application compatibility, vendor contracts and operational resilience.

This demands cryptographic agility: the ability to replace or adapt cryptographic mechanisms without rebuilding the enterprise.

The same architectural discipline applies to future quantum workloads.

Enterprises should favor modular integration, well-defined interfaces, workload portability and interoperability across classical computing, high-performance computing, AI and emerging quantum services.

Quantum will not make classical computing obsolete. The more credible architectural direction is selective integration where a quantum capability demonstrably improves a specific computational outcome.

The architectural objective therefore is not quantum dependence. It is quantum optionality.

An enterprise should be able to adopt a useful breakthrough without surrendering control of its technology economics or becoming captive to a single provider.

The missing equation: Quantum workload economics

The quantum conversation becomes strategically meaningful when CIOs stop asking what a quantum computer can theoretically perform and start asking what business outcome it can improve.

The OECD’s 2026 research, Building Business Readiness for Quantum Computing, identifies barriers including technological immaturity, uncertainty surrounding business applications, access and training costs, and shortages of specialized expertise.

These are not simply engineering obstacles. They are capital allocation constraints. This means that a quantum experiment may demonstrate technical progress while failing to establish commercial value.

For example, a proposed optimization workload should be evaluated against competitive classical algorithms, realistic datasets, operational constraints and the full cost of execution.

The comparison must include more than processing time. It should consider problem preparation, data movement, orchestration, error mitigation or correction, integration, specialized talent, assurance and recurring operating expenses.

Even an impressive laboratory result may offer little economic benefit if the end-to-end enterprise workflow becomes slower, costlier or less dependable.

I would therefore introduce a more demanding investment metric: Cost per Trusted Quantum-Enabled Business Outcome.

This proposed measure evaluates the total attributable cost of achieving a validated business result, including the controls necessary to make that result operationally acceptable.

The denominator is not the number of quantum circuits executed. It is the number of useful, verified business outcomes delivered.

Where no defensible quantum advantage exists, the responsible decision may be to continue using classical computing.

That is not technological conservatism. It is capital discipline.

Introducing the quantum capital discipline framework

I propose a six-dimensional executive framework for separating quantum preparedness from quantum speculation.

  1. Exposure: What must we protect? Identify vulnerable cryptographic dependencies, long-lived sensitive information, critical services and contractual or regulatory obligations. Prioritize remediation by business consequence, not technology fashion.
  2. Relevance: What problem warrants quantum? Establish a specific business problem whose computational characteristics plausibly justify quantum investigation. Scientific curiosity alone is not an enterprise investment thesis.
  3. Advantage: What evidence proves improvement? Demand reproducible comparisons against strong classical alternatives. Evaluate solution quality, performance, operational constraints and independent validation.
  4. Architecture: Can we adapt without lock-in? Assess portability, integration complexity, vendor concentration, reversibility and the ability to change technology choices as the market evolves.
  5. Economics: What is the full cost of value? Measure total lifecycle costs, opportunity costs, talent requirements and credible returns. Distinguish research expenditure from production investment.
  6. Authority: Who decides to advance, defer or stop? Assign accountable decision makers, measurable milestones, investment thresholds and explicit exit criteria. Together, these dimensions form the Quantum Capital Discipline Framework.

Its governing principle is straightforward:

Capital follows evidence. Architecture preserves options. Governance owns consequences.

Importantly, this framework does not subject essential cryptographic remediation to the same commercial-return requirements as speculative quantum workloads. Security obligations and innovation opportunities require different investment justifications.

What boards should demand from their CIOs

Quantum strategy should enter Board discussions through enterprise risk, capital allocation, resilience and competitive positioning — not promotional demonstrations.

I would encourage directors and executive committees to demand answers to five key questions:

  1. Which critical business services and information assets face material quantum-related cryptographic exposure?
  2. Can we modernize vulnerable dependencies without unacceptable operational disruption?
  3. Which proposed quantum applications outperform credible classical alternatives?
  4. What evidence would justify expanding, delaying or terminating quantum investments?
  5. Who is accountable for the financial, security and architectural consequences?

These five questions create a practical governance boundary between preparedness and speculation. They also expose a broader institutional weakness: enterprises often approve emerging technology investments without establishing the conditions under which those investments should be reconsidered.

Quantum requires a different approach.

Investment decisions should be revisited when technical capabilities, benchmark results, standards, security exposure or business economics materially change.

Boards should insist on measurable progress but avoid manufacturing artificial deadlines for breakthroughs nobody can reliably predict.

The CIO’s next mandate: Preserve the freedom to act

Quantum computing will not transform every industry simultaneously, deliver equal advantage across workloads or reward every early investor.

Some enterprises may eventually realize significant value from specialized quantum applications. Others may encounter quantum’s most immediate consequences through cryptographic modernization, technology dependencies and the protection of long-lived information.

Both outcomes demand leadership today.

The CIO’s responsibility is not to predict which quantum architecture will prevail or which vendor will dominate. It is to ensure that today’s decisions do not compromise tomorrow’s ability to compete, adapt and protect enterprise trust.

That requires investment discipline, architectural foresight, credible experimentation and accountable governance.

The next quantum advantage may belong not to the enterprise that invests first or spends the most, but to the one that knows precisely when to act, where to invest and when to walk away.

Quantum readiness is not measured by the technology an enterprise owns. It is measured by the strategic freedom it retains, the risks it responsibly reduces and the business value it can demonstrably create.

That is the difference between quantum enthusiasm and quantum leadership.

Quantum leadership is not about predicting when the future arrives. It is about architecting the freedom to embrace it, exercising the discipline to invest in it and preserving the authority to walk away when promise fails to become value.
